query: FeNiCrCoCu is considered suitable for thin-film use, and its expense favors applying it as a protective coating on conventional metals rather than using it in bulk. Earlier studies examined room-temperature wear behavior in relation to coating–substrate combinations, composition, and grain size, but largely addressed the alloy itself or a limited thermal regime rather than the overall wear response of a coating across different temperatures. Under the constraints that FeNiCrCoCu remains a thin protective coating and that high-temperature wear is the target application, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its overall wear resistance and why? Specify an intervention relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the observations expected if the hypothesis is correct, state the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, connect the hypothesis to prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The high-temperature wear resistance of FeNiCrCoCu thin coatings is governed by the formation and mechanical integrity of an in-situ Cr-rich oxide tribofilm whose growth kinetics and cohesion are enhanced by a nanocrystalline grain structure, leading to reduced material removal under load.
generation.material_initial_state: Baseline FeNiCrCoCu coating deposited to yield an average grain size of ~500 nm.
generation.intervention: Modify deposition parameters (e.g., increased substrate bias and reduced temperature) to produce a nanocrystalline coating with average grain size <50 nm.
generation.conditions: Wear tests in air at 500–800 °C under normal loads of 1–10 N; sliding speed ~10 mm/s.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain-boundary-mediated rapid supply of Cr to the surface, producing a continuous, adherent Cr₂O₃ layer.
generation.mechanism: Nanocrystalline grain structure enhances short‐circuit diffusion of Cr to the surface, forming a coherent oxide tribofilm that carries the majority of the load and reduces direct metal‐metal contact.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanocrystalline coatings will exhibit a steady‐state wear rate 30–70% lower than the baseline (~500 nm grain) coatings and display a continuous, adherent Cr₂O₃ top layer in post‐test surface analyses.
generation.baseline: ~500 nm‐grain FeNiCrCoCu coating under the same test conditions.
generation.boundary: Valid for temperatures between 500 and 800 °C, normal loads from 1 to 10 N, sliding speeds around 10 mm/s; outside these ranges, oxide kinetics or mechanical behavior may change.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the wear‐rate reduction may vary with minor deviations in environmental humidity or exact film chemistry; continuity of the oxide film may also depend on the sliding regime.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two FeNiCrCoCu coatings on the same substrate: one nanocrystalline (<50 nm) and one microcrystalline (~500 nm). Perform high‐temperature pin-on-disk wear tests at 700 °C, 5 N load, 10 mm/s sliding in air. Characterize post‐wear surfaces by SEM/EDS and XPS for oxide continuity and composition.
measurements: Thickness and continuity of surface oxide layer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nanocrystalline coating does not show ≥20% lower steady-state wear rate than the baseline or does not form a more continuous Cr₂O₃ film (as quantified by >15% higher surface oxide coverage), then the hypothesis is falsified.
